chapters.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: As for what you're asking about, I believe I'm well prepared to answer. In fact, the day before yesterday I was on my way into the city from my home in Phalerum when an acquaintance of mine caught sight of me from behind and called out playfully from a distance, 'Apollodorus! You there — you Phalerian! Halt!' So I did as I was told, and he said, 'Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I wanted to ask you about the speeches in praise of love that Socrates, Alcibiades, and others gave at Agathon's supper. Someone told me what he had heard from Phoenix, the son of Philip, but his account was very vague. He did say, though, that you knew about them, so I'd like to hear them from you. Who better than you to report your friend's words? But first tell me,' he said, 'were you at that gathering yourself?'
'Glaucon,' I said, 'your informant must have been very vague indeed, if you imagine that the occasion was recent, or that I could have been one of the party.'
'Well, yes,' he replied, 'I did think so.'

'Impossible,' I said. 'Don't you know that Agathon hasn't lived in Athens for many years, and that it's not yet three years since I started spending time with Socrates and made it my daily business to know everything he says and does? There was a time when I ran around from one thing to another, thinking I was doing something worthwhile, but I was really a thoroughly wretched creature — no better than you are now. I thought I ought to do anything rather than be a philosopher.'
'Well,' he said, 'joking aside, tell me when that gathering took place.'
'When we were still boys,' I replied, 'at the time Agathon won the prize with his first tragedy. It was the day after he and his chorus had offered their victory sacrifice.'
'Then it must have been a long time ago,' he said. 'And who told you — was it Socrates?'

'No, not Socrates,' I replied. 'It was the same man who told Phoenix — Aristodemus, of the deme of Cydathenaeum, a little fellow who never wore shoes. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one was a more devoted admirer of Socrates. What's more, I have asked Socrates himself whether some parts of Aristodemus's account were true, and he confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let's hear the story. Isn't the road to Athens just made for conversation?' So we walked along and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I told you at the start, I'm well prepared to do what you ask; I'll go through them again for you, if you like. For speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak about it, always gives me the greatest pleasure — to say nothing of the benefit. But when I hear any other kind of talk — especially the talk of rich men and businessmen like you — it annoys me; and I pity you, my friends, because you think you're doing something when in reality you're doing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return and think I'm miserable — and very probably you're right. But what you only think about me, I know for certain about you. That's the difference.

COMPANION: I see you're just the same as ever, Apollodorus — always speaking ill of yourself and of others. I really do believe you pity all mankind except Socrates, starting with yourself. In this you live up to your old nickname, 'Apollodorus the madman.' I don't know how you came by it, but it suits you, for you're always raging against yourself and everybody except Socrates.
APOLLODORUS: Yes, friend, and the reason people say I'm crazy and out of my mind is precisely because I hold these views about you and about myself. No other evidence is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Let me renew my request and ask you to repeat the conversation for me.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the tale of love went like this — but perhaps I should start from the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus.

He said that he met Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing sandals — and as the sight of the sandals was unusual, he asked him where he was going, that he had turned himself into such a fine figure.

'To a banquet at Agathon's,' he replied. 'I turned down his invitation yesterday — his victory sacrifice — because I was afraid of a crowd, but I promised to come today instead. So I've put on my finery, because he's such a fine man. What do you say — will you come along unasked?'
'I'll do as you bid me,' I replied.
'Follow me, then,' he said, 'and let's demolish the proverb:'
'To the feasts of inferior men the good unbidden go;'
and instead our proverb will run:
'To the feasts of the good the good unbidden go;'

and this alteration can be supported by the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes but literally outrages the proverb. After picturing Agamemnon as the most valiant of men, he has Menelaus — who is only a fainthearted warrior — come unbidden to Agamemnon's banquet, the man who was feasting and offering sacrifices: so the worse comes to the better, not the better to the worse.
'I'm rather afraid, Socrates,' said Aristodemus, 'that this may still be my case — that, like Menelaus in Homer, I shall be the inferior person who',
'To the feasts of the wise unbidden goes.'
But I shall say that I was bidden of you, and then you'll have to make an excuse for me.
'Two going together,'
he replied, in Homeric fashion, 'one or other of them may invent an excuse by the way.'

This was the style of their conversation as they went along. Then Socrates dropped behind in a fit of abstraction and told Aristodemus, who was waiting for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached the house of Agathon, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him at once into the banqueting hall, where the guests were already reclining, for the banquet was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You are just in time to sup with us. If you come on any other matter, put it off and make one of us — I was looking for you yesterday and meant to have asked you, if I could have found you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
I turned round, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. So I had to explain that he had been with me only a moment before, and that I had come by his invitation to the supper.
'You were quite right in coming,' said Agathon, 'but where is he himself?'
'He was behind me just now, as I entered,' he said, 'and I can't think what has become of him.'
'Go and look for him, boy,' said Agathon, 'and bring him in. And you, Aristodemus, take the place by Eryximachus in the meantime.'

The servant then assisted him to wash, and he lay down. Presently another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had retired into the portico of the neighboring house. 'There he is fixed,' the servant said, 'and when I call to him he will not stir.'
'How strange,' said Agathon. 'Then you must call him again, and keep calling him.'
'Let him alone,' said my informant. 'He has a way of stopping anywhere and losing himself without any reason. I believe he will soon appear — do not therefore disturb him.'

'Well, if you think so, I will leave him,' said Agathon. And then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Let us have supper without waiting for him. Serve up whatever you please, for there is no one to give you orders; up until now I have never left you to yourselves, but on this occasion imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and then we shall commend you.' After this, supper was served, but still no Socrates. During the meal Agathon several times expressed a wish to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over — for the fit, as usual, was not of long duration — Socrates entered. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him. ''I may touch you,' he said, 'and have the benefit of that wise thought which came into your mind in the portico, and is now in your possession — for I am certain that you would not have come away until you had found what you sought.''

'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking his place as he was desired, 'that wisdom could be infused by touch, out of the fuller into the emptier man, as water runs through wool out of a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how greatly should I value the privilege of reclining at your side! For you would have filled me full with a stream of wisdom plenteous and fair — whereas my own is of a very mean and questionable sort, no better than a dream. But yours is bright and full of promise, and was manifested forth in all the splendor of youth the day before yesterday, in the presence of more than thirty thousand Greeks.'

'You are mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'and before long you and I will have to determine who bears off the palm of wisdom — of this Dionysus shall be the judge. But at present you are better occupied with supper.'

Socrates took his place on the couch, and supped with the rest. Then libations were offered, and after a hymn had been sung to the god, and the usual ceremonies completed, they were about to commence drinking when Pausanias said, 'And now, my friends, how can we drink with the least injury to ourselves? I can assure you that I feel severely the effects of yesterday's potations, and must have time to recover; and I suspect that most of you are in the same predicament, for you were of the party yesterday. Consider, then: how can the drinking be made easiest?'
'I entirely agree,' said Aristophanes, 'that we should by all means avoid hard drinking, for I was myself one of those who were yesterday drowned in drink.'
'I think that you are right,' said Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus. 'But I should still like to hear one other person speak: is Agathon able to drink hard?'
'I am not equal to it,' said Agathon.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'the weak heads like myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who never can drink, are fortunate in finding that the stronger ones are not in a drinking mood. I do not include Socrates, who is able either to drink or to abstain, and will not mind whichever we do. Well, as none of the company seem disposed to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that drinking deep is a bad practice, which I never follow if I can help it, and certainly do not recommend to another — least of all to any one who still feels the effects of yesterday's carouse.'
'I always do what you advise, and especially what you prescribe as a physician,' rejoined Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian, 'and the rest of the company, if they are wise, will do the same.'
It was agreed that drinking was not to be the order of the day, but that they were all to drink only so much as they pleased.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'as you are all agreed that drinking is to be voluntary, and that there is to be no compulsion, I move in the next place that the flute-girl, who has just made her appearance, be told to go away and play to herself, or, if she likes, to the women who are within. Today let us have conversation instead; and, if you will allow me, I will tell you what sort of conversation.' This proposal having been accepted, Eryximachus proceeded as follows:
'I will begin,' he said, 'after the manner of Melanippe in Euripides,'
'Not mine the word —'

'which I am about to speak, but that of Phaedrus. For often he says to me in an indignant tone: What a strange thing it is, Eryximachus, that whereas other gods have poems and hymns made in their honor, the great and glorious god Love has no encomiast among all the poets who are so many. There are the worthy sophists too — the excellent Prodicus, for example, who have descanted in prose on the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And, what is still more extraordinary, I have met with a philosophical work in which the utility of salt has been made the theme of an eloquent discourse, and many other like things have had a like honor bestowed upon them. And only to think that there should have been such eager interest created about them, and yet that to this day no one has ever dared worthily to hymn Love's praises! So entirely has this great deity been neglected. Now in this Phaedrus seems to me quite right, and therefore I want to offer him a contribution. Also I think that at the present moment we who are here assembled cannot do better than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, there will be no lack of conversation, for I mean to propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, shall make a speech in honor of Love — let him give us the best which he can; and Phaedrus, because he is sitting first on the left hand, and because he is the father of the thought, shall begin.'

'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How can I oppose your motion, who profess to understand nothing but matters of love? Nor, I presume, will Agathon and Pausanias — and there can be no doubt of Aristophanes, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite. Nor will anyone disagree of those whom I see around me. The proposal, as I am aware, may seem rather hard on those of us whose place is last; but we shall be content if we hear some good speeches first. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company expressed their assent and desired him to do as Socrates bade him.
Aristodemus did not recollect all that was said, nor do I recollect all that he related to me; but I will tell you what I thought most worthy of remembrance, and what the chief speakers said.

chapters.title: Phaedrus's Speech
paragraphs: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a powerful god, a wonder to gods and human beings alike, and most wonderful of all in his birth. He is the oldest of the gods, and that gives him honour. The evidence for this claim is that no record of his parents exists: no poet or prose writer has ever said he had any. As Hesiod puts it:
'First Chaos came, and then broad-bosomed Earth, The everlasting seat of all that is, And Love.'
That is, after Chaos, these two came into existence: Earth and Love. Parmenides, too, sings of Generation:
'First in the train of gods, he fashioned Love.'

And Acusilaus agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who recognise Love as the oldest god. He is not only the oldest, but also the source of our greatest blessings. I know of no greater blessing for a young man just beginning life than a virtuous lover, or for a lover than a beloved youth. There is a principle that should guide anyone who wants to live nobly, and neither family, honour, wealth, nor any other motive can establish it as well as love. What principle do I mean? The sense of honour and dishonour, without which neither cities nor individuals ever accomplish anything good or great. I say that if a lover is caught doing something dishonourable, or cowardly submitting to dishonour at someone else’s hands, being discovered by his beloved will hurt him more than being seen by his father, his companions, or anyone else. A beloved youth caught in some disgrace feels just the same about his lover. If only we could arrange for a city or an army to consist of lovers and their beloveds (compare Rep.), they would govern their city in the best possible way, avoiding every dishonour and competing to outdo one another in honour. Fighting side by side, even a handful of them could defeat the world.

For what lover, abandoning his post or throwing away his weapons, would not rather be seen by the whole human race than by his beloved? He would willingly die a thousand deaths rather than bear that. And who would abandon his beloved or fail him in a moment of danger? Even the greatest coward would then become an inspired hero, as brave as the bravest: Love would inspire him. The courage that a god breathes into certain heroes’ souls, as Homer says, is what Love, by his own nature, pours into the lover.

Love alone makes people dare to die for those they love—women as well as men. Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, stands as an example of this to all Hellas. She was willing to give her life for her husband when no one else would, although he had both a father and a mother. Her tender love so far surpassed theirs that she made them look like strangers to their own son, related to him only in name and not by blood. Both gods and human beings found her action so noble that, among the many who have acted virtuously, she is one of the very few whom the gods, admiring her noble deed, allowed to return alive to earth. Such extraordinary honour do the gods give to love’s devotion and virtue. But they sent the harpist Orpheus, son of Oeagrus, away empty-handed. They showed him only an apparition of the woman he sought and refused to release the woman herself, because he had shown no spirit. He was merely a harp-player: rather than dare, like Alcestis, to die for love, he schemed to enter Hades alive. What is more, they later punished his cowardice by making him die at the hands of women.

How different was the reward for Achilles’ true love of his lover Patroclus—his lover, not his beloved. Aeschylus foolishly gets this wrong in treating Patroclus as the beloved: Achilles was certainly the more beautiful of the two, and more beautiful than all the other heroes as well; besides, Homer tells us he was still beardless and much younger. Great as the gods’ respect for love’s virtue is, they admire, value, and reward still more the love a beloved returns to his lover, because the lover is the more divine, inspired as he is by God. Achilles knew perfectly well from his mother that he could escape death, return home, and reach a good old age if he refrained from killing Hector. Yet he gave his life to avenge his friend, daring to die not only in his defence but after his death. The gods therefore honoured him even more than Alcestis, sending him to the Islands of the Blest. These are my reasons for saying that Love is the oldest, noblest, and most powerful of the gods, and the greatest source and giver of virtue during life and happiness after death.

chapters.title: Pausanias's Speech
paragraphs: This, or something close to it, was Phaedrus's speech. Several other speeches followed that Aristodemus couldn't remember, but the next one he recounted was Pausanias's. Pausanias began: Phaedrus, I don't think the question has been framed correctly. We shouldn't be asked to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be fine — but since there are more Loves than one, we should have started by deciding which of them we are praising. Let me fix this oversight. First I'll tell you which Love deserves our praise, and then I'll try to hymn that praiseworthy one in a manner worthy of him. For we all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love — but since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder, who has no mother, is called the heavenly Aphrodite — she is the daughter of Uranus. The younger, the daughter of Zeus and Dione, we call Common; and the Love who works alongside her is rightly named Common, just as the other Love is called Heavenly. All the gods deserve praise, but not without distinguishing their natures — so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now, actions vary in value according to how they are performed.

Take, for example, what we are doing right now — drinking, singing, and talking. These actions are not in themselves either good or evil; they turn out one way or the other depending on how they are done. Done well, they are good; done badly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise — only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the offspring of the Common Aphrodite is essentially common and makes no distinctions. It is the love the meaner sort of men feel, directed equally at women and at youths, and it is of the body rather than the soul. The most foolish beings are the objects of this love, which cares only about getting what it wants and never about achieving its end nobly, and so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is far younger than the other, and she was born of the union of male and female, partaking of both. But the offspring of the Heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female had no part — she is from the male only. This is the love that is directed toward youths, and because the goddess is older, there is nothing of wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, delighting in whoever has the more valiant and intelligent nature; and anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts by the very character of their attachments.

For they love not boys, but intelligent beings whose reason is beginning to develop — around the age when their beards begin to grow. And in choosing young men as their companions, they mean to be faithful to them, to spend their whole lives with them — not to catch them in their inexperience, deceive them, play the fool with them, or run from one to another. The love of young boys, however, ought to be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain: they may turn out good or bad, in body or soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force — just as we try to restrain them from fixing their affections on freeborn women. These are the people who bring reproach upon love; and some have been led to deny the lawfulness of such attachments altogether because they see the impropriety and evil in them. But surely nothing done decorously and lawfully can justly be censured.

Now here in Athens, and in Lacedaemon, the rules about love are perplexing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to grasp. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries that have no gift for eloquence, the rules are very straightforward — the law is simply in favor of these connections, and no one, young or old, says a word against them. The reason, I suppose, is that the men there are not eloquent, so lovers prefer not to take the trouble of pleading their case. In Ionia, on the other hand, and in other places generally subject to the barbarians, the custom is held to be dishonorable. There, love between males shares the evil reputation attached to philosophy and gymnastics, because all three are hostile to tyranny. Rulers' interests require that their subjects be poor in spirit and that no strong bond of friendship or fellowship form among them — and love, more than any other motive, is likely to inspire such bonds, as our own Athenian tyrants learned by experience. For Aristogeiton's love and Harmodius's constancy proved strong enough to bring down their power.

And so the ill repute into which these attachments have fallen in some places must be attributed to the bad character of those who condemn them — that is, to the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. On the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in other countries is owing to the mental laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, though, as I said, it's a rather perplexing one. Consider: open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and the love of the noblest and highest is especially honorable, even when the beloved is less beautiful than others. Consider too the enormous encouragement the whole world gives the lover: he is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable — if he succeeds he is praised, and if he fails he is blamed. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things that philosophy would bitterly condemn if they were done from any motive of profit, or desire for office, or power.

He may pray, beg, supplicate, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a servitude worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of meanness or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear and forswear himself — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then again — when fathers forbid their sons to speak with their lovers and place them under a tutor whose job is to prevent any such thing, and when their companions and peers taunt them for anything of the sort they observe, and their elders refuse to silence these reproaches or rebuke them — anyone reflecting on all this would, on the contrary, conclude that we hold these practices to be utterly disgraceful.

But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding to the bad, or yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to the good, or yielding in an honorable way. Evil is the vulgar lover, who loves the body rather than the soul — he isn't even stable, because he loves something that is itself unstable, so when the bloom of youth he desired is gone, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his words and promises. But the love of a noble disposition lasts a lifetime, for it becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country would have both lover and beloved thoroughly tested — have us yield to the one sort of lover and avoid the other, and therefore it encourages some to pursue and others to flee, testing both the lover and the beloved in contests and trials until it becomes clear which class each of them belongs to.

This is why, in the first place, a hasty attachment is considered dishonorable: time is the true test, here as in most other things. And secondly, there is dishonor in being overcome by the love of money, wealth, or political power — whether a man is frightened into surrender by the fear of losing them, or, having tasted the benefits of money and political corruption, cannot rise above their seductions. For none of these things is permanent or lasting, and besides, no generous friendship ever sprang from them. There remains, then, only one honorable way, allowed by custom, for the beloved to yield — the way of virtue. For just as we granted that any service the lover renders to his beloved is not to be counted as flattery or as a dishonor to himself, so the beloved has one, and only one, form of voluntary service that is not dishonorable: namely, virtuous service.

For we have a custom according to which, if someone serves another in the belief that he will be improved by him — whether in wisdom or in some other particular of virtue — such voluntary service is not to be considered a dishonor, and it is not open to the charge of flattery. These two customs — the love of youth, and the practice of philosophy and virtue generally — ought to meet in one; and when they do, the beloved may honorably yield to the lover. For when lover and beloved come together, each following his own law: the lover thinking he is right to do any service he can for his gracious loved one, and the beloved thinking he is right to show any kindness he can to the one who is making him wise and good — the first capable of communicating wisdom and virtue, the second seeking to acquire them for the sake of his education and wisdom — then, when the two laws of love are fulfilled and meet in one, and only then, may the beloved yield honorably to the lover. And when love is of this disinterested sort, there is no disgrace in being deceived; but in every other case there is equal disgrace in being deceived or not. For if someone yields to a lover under the impression that he is rich, and is then disappointed of his gains because the lover turns out to be poor, he is disgraced just the same — because he has done his best to show that he would give himself up to anyone's 'uses base' for the sake of money; and that is not honorable.

By the same principle, a man who gives himself to a lover because he believes him to be a good man, hoping to be improved by his company, shows himself to be virtuous even if the object of his affection turns out to be a scoundrel with no virtue at all. If he is deceived, his error is a noble one. For he has proved that on his side he will do anything for anyone with a view to virtue and self-improvement — and nothing can be nobler than that. Noble, then, in every case, is the acceptance of another for the sake of virtue. This is the love of the Heavenly Goddess — heavenly love, of great worth to individuals and to cities, making lover and beloved alike earnest in the work of their own improvement. All other loves are the offspring of the other goddess, the Common one. To you, Phaedrus, I offer this contribution of mine in praise of Love, the best I could make on short notice.

Pausanias came to a pause — this is the balanced way of speaking I've been taught by the wise. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was supposed to speak next, but either from eating too much or for some other reason he had the hiccups and had to switch turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch just below him. Eryximachus, he said, you ought either to cure my hiccups or speak in my turn until they stop.

I'll do both, said Eryximachus. I'll speak in your place, and you can speak in mine; and while I'm speaking, let me recommend you hold your breath. If after a while the hiccups haven't gotten better, then gargle a little water; and if they still persist, tickle your nose with something and sneeze — once or twice should do it, and even the most violent hiccups are sure to stop. I'll do as you prescribe, said Aristophanes. Now get on with it.

chapters.title: Eryximachus's Speech
paragraphs: Eryximachus spoke next: Pausanias began well but came to a rather weak conclusion, so I must try to supply what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. My own art, however, teaches me that this double love is not simply a feeling in the human soul towards beauty, or towards anything else. It exists in the bodies of every animal, in everything the earth produces, and, I might say, in everything that exists. That is the conclusion I believe I have drawn from my own art of medicine. It teaches me how great, wonderful, and universal the god of love is, ruling over all things, human and divine alike. I will begin with medicine to do my art honour. These two kinds of love exist in the human body and are admittedly different and unlike. Because they are unlike, their loves and desires differ too: what is healthy desires one thing, what is diseased another. Just as Pausanias was saying that it is honourable to satisfy good men but dishonourable to satisfy bad ones, so in the body we should satisfy its good and healthy elements, while discouraging, rather than satisfying, its bad and diseased elements.

This is the physician’s task and the substance of the art of medicine. Broadly speaking, medicine is knowledge of the body’s loves and desires and of when to satisfy them or withhold satisfaction. The best physician can distinguish noble love from ugly love or turn one into the other. A skilled practitioner knows how to remove love or introduce it, as needed, and how to reconcile the most hostile elements in our constitution and make them loving friends. The most hostile elements are the greatest opposites: hot and cold, bitter and sweet, wet and dry, and so on. My ancestor Asclepius knew how to establish friendship and agreement among these elements and so created our art, as our poet friends here tell us, and I believe them. Not only every branch of medicine but also gymnastics and husbandry fall under his rule. Anyone who gives the matter even a little attention will see the same reconciliation of opposites in music. This, I suppose, is what Heracleitus meant, although he did not express it accurately. He says that The One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre. Yet it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it consists of elements still in disagreement.

What he probably meant is that harmony consists of different high and low notes that once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. If those high and low notes still disagreed, there plainly could be no harmony. Harmony is a symphony, and a symphony is an agreement; but disagreements cannot agree while they remain in disagreement. You cannot harmonise what disagrees. Similarly, rhythm combines short and long elements that once differed and now agree. Just as medicine established agreement in the previous case, music establishes it in all these others, making love and unity grow between the elements. Music, then, also deals with the principles of love as they apply to harmony and rhythm. In harmony and rhythm considered in themselves, it is easy to recognise love, which has not yet divided into two kinds. But difficulty begins when you want to apply them in actual life, either by composing songs or by correctly performing melodies or metres already composed—the latter being called education. That is when a good artist is needed.

Then we must tell the old story again: of noble, heavenly love, the love of Urania, the noble and heavenly muse; of our duty to welcome the temperate, and to welcome those not yet temperate only so that they may become so, preserving their love. We must also speak of the common Polyhymnia, who needs careful handling so that we enjoy the pleasure without producing licentiousness. In my own art, similarly, it is a great achievement to regulate a gourmet’s desires so that he can indulge his tastes without suffering the evil of disease along with them. I conclude that in music, medicine, and everything else, human or divine, we should pay as much attention as possible to both loves, since both are present.

Both principles also pervade the cycle of the seasons. When, as I was saying, hot and cold, wet and dry reach a harmonious love for one another and blend with moderation and harmony, they bring health and abundance to human beings, animals, and plants, harming none of them. But when wanton love gains control and influences the year’s seasons, it is terribly destructive and harmful. It causes pestilence and many other diseases in animals and plants. Hoar-frost, hail, and blight arise from excess and disorder in these elements of love; knowledge of them in relation to the movements of the heavenly bodies and the seasons is called astronomy. Furthermore, every sacrifice and the entire field of divination—the art of communication between gods and human beings—are concerned solely with preserving good love and curing evil love. All kinds of impiety may arise when someone honours the other love instead of welcoming, honouring, and revering harmonious love in all his actions, whether towards gods or parents, the living or the dead. Divination must therefore attend to these loves and heal them. It makes peace between gods and human beings by understanding the religious and irreligious tendencies within human loves. Such is the great and mighty—or rather all-powerful—force of love in general.

Above all, the love directed towards goodness, brought to perfection alongside temperance and justice among gods or human beings, has the greatest power. It gives us all our happiness and harmony and makes us friends both with one another and with the gods above us. I dare say I too have left out several things that could be said in Love’s praise, though not deliberately. You, Aristophanes, can now fill the gap, or take a different approach to praising him, since I see your hiccups have stopped.

Yes, said Aristophanes, speaking next, the hiccups have gone—but only after I tried sneezing. It makes me wonder whether bodily harmony has a love for such noises and tickling sensations, because no sooner had I brought on a sneeze than I was cured.

Eryximachus replied: Take care, my friend Aristophanes. Your turn to speak is coming, yet you are making fun of me. I shall have to keep watch for a chance to laugh at your expense, when you could have delivered your speech in peace.

You are right, said Aristophanes with a laugh. I take back what I said. But please do not keep watch on me. I am afraid that in the speech I am about to give, people will merely laugh at me rather than laugh with me—the latter would suit our muse’s native manner and be much better.
Do you think you can fire your shot and get away, Aristophanes? Well, perhaps I can be persuaded to let you off, if you take great care and remember that you will have to answer for yourself.

chapters.title: Aristophanes's Speech
paragraphs: Aristophanes announced that he would take a different line of argument. He wanted to praise Love in his own way, unlike either Pausanias or Eryximachus. Judging by how people neglect him, he said, I do not think humanity has ever understood Love’s power at all. If they understood it, they would surely build magnificent temples and altars and perform solemn sacrifices in his honour. They do none of this, though they certainly ought to: of all the gods, he is humanity’s best friend, our helper and the healer of the troubles that most obstruct our happiness as a race. I shall try to explain his power to you, and you can teach the rest of the world what I teach you. First, let me discuss human nature and what has happened to it, because our original nature was different from what it is today. Originally there were three sexes, not the present two: male, female, and a combination of both. This third kind had a name matching its double nature. It once really existed but has now disappeared; only the word 'Androgynous' survives, as an insult. Next, the original human being was round, with back and sides forming a circle. It had four hands and four feet, one head with two identical faces looking in opposite directions on a circular neck, four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else arranged to match.

It could walk upright as we do now, forwards or backwards as it chose. When it wanted to run fast, it could also roll over and over at great speed on its four hands and four feet—all eight together—like acrobats tumbling with their legs in the air. There were three sexes of the kind I have described because there are three heavenly parents: sun, moon, and earth. The male originally came from the sun, the female from the earth, and the male-female from the moon, which combines sun and earth. All were round and travelled in circles like their parents. Their strength and power were terrifying, their ambitions immense, and they attacked the gods. The story of Otys and Ephialtes concerns them: Homer says they dared to climb into heaven and would have seized the gods themselves. The heavenly council could not decide what to do. If the gods killed them and wiped out the race with thunderbolts, as they had the giants, the sacrifices and worship human beings offered would end. Yet the gods could not let their insolence go unchecked. At last, after much thought, Zeus found a solution. He said: 'Methinks I have a plan which will humble their pride and improve their manners; men shall continue to exist, but I will cut them in two and then they will be diminished in strength and increased in numbers; this will have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.

They shall walk upright on two legs, and if they continue insolent and will not be quiet, I will split them again and they shall hop about on a single leg.' Having said this, he cut human beings in half, as one halves a sorb-apple for pickling or divides an egg with a hair. As he cut each one, he told Apollo to turn its face and half its neck towards the cut, so that looking at its own severed surface would teach it humility. Apollo was also told to heal the wounds and reshape the bodies. He turned the face around and drew the skin from the sides over what we call the belly, like a drawstring purse. He left a single opening in the middle and tied it in a knot—the part we call the navel. He shaped the chest too, smoothing out most of the wrinkles as a shoemaker smooths leather over a last. He did leave a few around the belly and navel as a reminder of the original condition. After the division, each half longed for its other half. They came together, threw their arms around one another, and clung in an embrace, wanting to grow back into one. Unwilling to do anything separately, they came close to dying of hunger and self-neglect. If one half died and the other remained alive, the survivor searched for another partner, male or female as we call them—sections of whole males or females—and clung to that one instead.

They were dying out when Zeus took pity and devised another plan. He moved their reproductive organs to the front, where they had not always been, so that instead of planting seed in the ground like grasshoppers, they planted it in one another. After this change, the male reproduced within the female: when man and woman embraced, they could have children and keep the race alive; when man embraced man, they could find satisfaction, rest, and return to life’s business. That is how ancient our implanted desire for one another is: it reunites our original nature, makes one out of two, and heals the human condition. Each of us, separated and left with only one side like a flatfish, is merely the matching fragment, the indenture, of a human being, always searching for the other half. Men cut from the double nature once called Androgynous love women; adulterers mostly come from this kind, as do adulterous women who desire men. Women cut from an original woman have no interest in men but form attachments to women; female companions belong to this kind. Those cut from a male pursue males. While young, being slices of the original man, they seek men’s company and embrace them, and they are the best boys and youths because their nature is the most manly.

Some call them shameless, but that is simply not true. They do not act this way for lack of shame: they are courageous and manly, with a manly bearing, and they embrace what resembles them. The strongest proof of what I say is that these alone grow up to become our statesmen. As adults they love youths and have no natural wish to marry or father children. If they do so at all, it is only to obey the law; they are content if allowed to live together unmarried. Such a person readily loves and returns love, always embracing what is akin to him. When one of them meets his other half, the actual half of himself—whether he loves youths or loves in some other way—the two are overwhelmed with love, friendship, and intimacy, unwilling, one might say, to let each other out of sight for even a moment. These are people who spend their whole lives together, yet could not explain what they want from each other. Their intense mutual longing does not seem to be a desire for lovers’ intercourse. Each soul plainly desires something else, something she cannot express and only dimly, uncertainly senses.

Imagine Hephaestus arriving with his tools while the two lie beside each other, and asking, 'What do you people want of one another?' They could not explain. Imagine that, seeing their confusion, he went on: 'Do you desire to be wholly one; always day and night to be in one another’s company? for if this is what you desire, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that being two you shall become one, and while you live live a common life as if you were a single man, and after your death in the world below still be one departed soul instead of two—I ask whether this is what you lovingly desire, and whether you are satisfied to attain this?' No one hearing this offer would reject it. Each would recognise this joining and melting together, this becoming one instead of two, as the exact expression of his ancient need (compare Arist. Pol.). The reason is that our human nature was originally one: we were whole, and love is the name for our desire and pursuit of that wholeness. Once, I say, we were one; now, because of humanity’s wickedness, God has scattered us, as the Lacedaemonians scattered the Arcadians into separate villages (compare Arist. Pol.).

If we fail to obey the gods, we risk being split once more, walking around in basso-relievo like the profile figures carved on monuments with only half a nose, reduced to tally halves. So let us urge everyone to be pious, so that we escape evil and obtain the good of which Love is our lord and minister. Let no one resist him: anyone who does is an enemy of the gods. If we are friends of the God and at peace with him, we shall find our true loves, something that rarely happens in today’s world. I am speaking seriously, and I must ask Eryximachus not to make fun of me or see a reference here to Pausanias and Agathon, whom I suspect are both of the manly nature and belong to the kind I have described. My words extend further: they include men and women everywhere. I believe our race would be happy if love were perfectly fulfilled and each of us returned to our original nature by finding our original true love. If that would be best of all, then the next best thing under present conditions must be whatever comes closest to that union: finding a love congenial to our nature.

If we wish, then, to praise the one who gives us this blessing, we must praise the god Love, our greatest benefactor. He leads us back towards our own nature in this life and gives us great hopes for the future, promising that if we are pious he will restore our original condition, heal us, and make us happy and blessed. That, Eryximachus, is my speech about love. Though it differs from yours, I ask you to spare it the arrows of your ridicule so that everyone can have a turn—everyone, or rather each of the two remaining speakers, since only Agathon and Socrates are left.

I certainly shall not attack you, said Eryximachus. I found your speech delightful. If I did not know that Agathon and Socrates are experts in love, I would genuinely fear they had nothing left to say after the wealth of things already said. Even so, I still have hopes.
Socrates said: You have played your part well, Eryximachus. But if you were in my position now—or rather, the position I shall be in after Agathon speaks—you really would be in trouble.
You are trying to put a spell on me, Socrates, said Agathon. You hope I will be unsettled by the audience’s heightened expectation of a fine speech from me.

Agathon, replied Socrates, I would have a very strange memory if I thought a small gathering of friends could shake your nerves. I remember your courage and noble spirit when your own compositions were about to be performed: you walked onstage with the actors and faced that enormous theatre without the slightest fear.
Do you think, Socrates, said Agathon, that I am so obsessed with the theatre that I fail to see how much more intimidating a few good judges are to a sensible person than a crowd of fools?

Certainly not, replied Socrates. I would be quite wrong to accuse you of that or any other lack of refinement, Agathon. I know perfectly well that if you encountered people you considered wise, their opinion would matter much more to you than the crowd’s. But since we were part of that foolish theatre crowd, we can hardly count as the select wise. Still, I know that if you found yourself before someone truly wise, rather than one of us, you would be ashamed to disgrace yourself in front of him—wouldn’t you?
Yes, Agathon replied.
But would you feel no shame before the crowd, if you thought you were doing something disgraceful in their presence?

Phaedrus interrupted: Do not answer him, my dear Agathon. Once he finds someone to talk to, especially someone good-looking, he will forget all about completing our programme. I love listening to him talk, but just at this moment I must remember the encomium on Love that he and everyone else owe me. Once you have both paid your tribute to the god, you may talk.

Very well, Phaedrus, said Agathon. I see no reason not to begin my speech, since there will be plenty of other chances to talk with Socrates. First let me explain how I should speak, and then I shall speak:

chapters.title: Agathon's Speech
paragraphs: The earlier speakers seem to have congratulated humanity on the benefits Love gives us, rather than praising the god himself or explaining his nature. I would prefer to praise the god first and then describe his gifts: that is always the proper order for praising anything. May I say, without impiety or offence, that of all the blessed gods he is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and best? He is the most beautiful because, first of all, he is the youngest. He proves his own youth by fleeing old age, swift though old age is—indeed, swifter than most of us would like. Love hates age and refuses to approach it, whereas youth and love live and move together: like to like, as the proverb says. I agree with much that Phaedrus said about Love, but not that he is older than Iapetus and Kronos. No: I maintain that he is the youngest god and remains forever young. If the ancient stories Hesiod and Parmenides tell about the gods are true, those deeds were the work of Necessity, not Love. Had Love existed then, there would have been no chaining or mutilating of gods, nor any other violence, but peace and gentleness, as there is now in heaven under Love’s rule. Love is young, and tender too. He deserves a poet like Homer to describe that tenderness. Homer calls Ate a goddess and describes her tenderness in these words:
'Her feet are tender, for she sets her steps, Not on the ground but on the heads of men:'

That gives excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks on soft things rather than hard ones. Let us offer similar evidence for Love’s tenderness. He walks neither on the earth nor on human skulls, which are hardly very soft, but in the hearts and souls of gods and human beings, the softest things of all. There he walks, lives, and makes his home. Not in every soul indiscriminately: where he finds hardness he leaves, and where he finds softness he stays. Always resting his feet and his whole being in the softest of soft places, how could he be anything but the softest of all? Truly, he is the tenderest as well as the youngest, and his form is supple too. If he were rigid and unbending, he could not enfold everything or slip unnoticed in and out of every human soul. His grace proves the suppleness and perfect proportions of his form: everyone agrees that grace belongs particularly to Love, while gracelessness and love are always enemies. His life among flowers reveals the beauty of his complexion. He never settles among faded beauties or those without bloom, whether of body, soul, or anything else; he sits and stays where flowers blossom and scents arise. I have said enough about the god’s beauty, though I could say much more.

Now I must speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he neither wrongs nor is wronged by any god or human being. Whatever he suffers, he does not suffer through force: force never approaches him, and he never uses force when he acts. Everyone serves him freely in everything, and voluntary agreement is justice, as the laws that rule the city declare. He is not only just but supremely temperate. Temperance is acknowledged to govern pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever overpowers Love: he is their master, and they serve him. If he conquers them, he must indeed be temperate. As for courage, even the God of War cannot match him. War is the captive and Love the master, since love—the love of Aphrodite—overcomes him, as the story tells. The master is stronger than his servant; if Love conquers the bravest of the rest, he must himself be bravest. I have spoken of his courage, justice, and temperance, but his wisdom remains. I must do my best to describe it within the limits of my ability. First, he is a poet—here, like Eryximachus, I honour my own art—and he inspires poetry in others, which he could not do without being a poet himself.

At his touch, everyone becomes a poet, even someone who previously had no music within him (A fragment of the Sthenoaoea of Euripides.). This too proves that Love is a good poet and skilled in every fine art, since no one can give what he does not possess or teach what he does not know. Who can deny that animals owe their creation to him? Are they not all products of his wisdom, born and begotten through him? And among artists, do we not know that only those inspired by love enjoy fame’s light? Anyone untouched by Love walks in darkness. Apollo discovered medicine, archery, and divination under the guidance of love and desire, making him another pupil of Love. The Muses’ music, Hephaestus’ metalworking, Athene’s weaving, and Zeus’ rule over gods and human beings likewise all come from Love, their inventor. In this way Love put the gods’ kingdom in order—love of beauty, clearly, since Love has nothing to do with deformity. As I said at the start, terrible deeds took place among the gods in ancient times because Necessity ruled them. But since Love’s birth, every good thing in heaven and on earth has arisen from love of the beautiful. So, Phaedrus, I call Love the most beautiful and best in himself, and the source of whatever is most beautiful and best in everything else. A line of poetry comes to mind, describing him as the god who
'Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, Who stills the winds and bids the sufferer sleep.'

He empties us of estrangement and fills us with affection, bringing us together at banquets like this one. At sacrifices, feasts, and dances he is our lord. He brings courtesy and banishes discourtesy, always giving kindness, never unkindness; friend of the good, wonder of the wise, marvel of the gods; longed for by those without a share in him, treasured by those with the richer share; father of delicacy, luxury, desire, fondness, softness, and grace; attentive to the good, indifferent to the evil. In every word, deed, wish, and fear, he is saviour, pilot, companion, and helper; the glory of gods and human beings, the finest and brightest leader. Let everyone follow his footsteps, singing sweetly in his honour, joining the sweet melody with which love enchants the souls of gods and human beings. Such, Phaedrus, is the speech I offer the god to the best of my ability: partly playful, yet with a measure of seriousness.

Aristodemus said that when Agathon finished, everyone cheered: the young man was thought to have spoken worthily of himself and the god. Socrates looked at Eryximachus and said: Tell me, son of Acumenus, were my fears not justified? Was I not a true prophet when I said Agathon would give a wonderful speech and leave me in difficulty?
The part of your prophecy about Agathon seems true to me, Eryximachus replied, but not the other part, about your being in difficulty.

My dear friend, said Socrates, how could I—or anyone—avoid difficulty when obliged to speak after hearing such a rich and varied address? The beauty of its closing words especially struck me: who could hear them without astonishment? Thinking how immeasurably inferior my own abilities were, I was ready to run away in shame, had escape been possible. It reminded me of Gorgias. At the speech’s end, I imagined Agathon brandishing that great master of rhetoric’s Gorginian—or Gorgonian—head at me, simply to turn me and my speech to stone, as Homer says (Odyssey), and leave me speechless. Then I realised how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn praising love with you, claiming that I too was an expert in the art, when I had no idea how anything should be praised. In my innocence, I thought praise ought to be true. Given that, a speaker should choose the best true things and present them as well as possible. I felt rather proud, imagining I understood true praise and would speak well. Now I see the intention was to award Love every kind of greatness and glory, whether or not he actually possessed it, without caring about truth or falsehood. That was irrelevant: apparently the original proposal was not that each of you should really praise Love, but merely seem to praise him.

So you heap on Love every imaginable tribute you can gather from anywhere. You say that 'he is all this,' and 'the cause of all that,' making him seem the most beautiful and best of all to people who do not know him, since you cannot deceive those who do. And what a noble, solemn hymn of praise you have performed. But when I agreed to take my turn, I misunderstood the kind of praise intended. I must therefore ask to be released from the promise I made in ignorance—a promise, as Euripides would say (Eurip. Hyppolytus), of the lips rather than the mind. Goodbye, then, to that style: I do not praise like that; indeed, I cannot. If, however, you want to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own way, without making myself ridiculous by competing with you. Tell me, Phaedrus: would you like the truth about love, expressed in whatever words and order happen to occur to me at the time? Would that suit you?

According to Aristodemus, Phaedrus and the others told him to speak in whatever way he thought best. Then, Socrates added, first allow me to ask Agathon a few more questions, so that I can use what he agrees to as the premises of my speech.
You have my permission, said Phaedrus; ask your questions. Socrates then began as follows:

chapters.title: Socrates & Diotima
paragraphs: My dear Agathon, in that magnificent speech you have just delivered, I think you were right to propose discussing Love’s nature first and his actions afterwards. I thoroughly approve of that way of beginning. Since you have described his nature so eloquently, may I ask a further question: is love love of something, or of nothing? Let me explain. I am not asking you to say that love is love of a father or a mother; that would be absurd. Answer as you would if I asked whether a father is the father of something. You would have no difficulty saying, of a son or daughter, and that answer would be correct.
Quite right, said Agathon.
And would you give the same answer about a mother?
He agreed.
Let me ask one further question to make my meaning clear: is a brother not, by his very nature, the brother of someone?
Of course, he replied.
Of a brother or a sister, that is?
Yes, he replied.
Now, said Socrates, let me ask about Love: does Love love something, or nothing?
Something, of course, he replied.
Remember what that something is, and answer this: does Love desire the thing of which he is the love?
Yes, of course.
And does he have the thing he loves and desires, or does he lack it?
I would say he probably lacks it.

No, replied Socrates, consider whether 'necessarily' is the better word. In my judgement, Agathon, it is absolutely and necessarily true that anyone who desires something lacks something, while anyone who desires nothing lacks nothing. That is what the argument implies. What do you think?
I agree with that, said Agathon.
Good. Would someone who is great desire to be great, or someone who is strong desire to be strong?
That would contradict what we have already agreed.
Exactly. Someone who already is something cannot lack what he is, can he?
That is quite true.

Yet, Socrates continued, if a strong man wanted to be strong, a swift man to be swift, or a healthy man to be healthy, we might think he wanted something he already had or already was. I offer these examples to prevent misunderstanding. Agathon, people possessing these qualities must have their respective advantages at that moment, whether they choose to or not; and who can desire what he already has? So when someone says, I am healthy and want to be healthy, or I am rich and want to be rich, and I simply want to have what I have, we shall reply: 'My friend, you have wealth, health, and strength, and you want them to continue. At this moment you possess them, whether you choose to or not. When you say you desire only what you already have, don’t you mean that you want to go on having it in the future?' He must agree with us, mustn’t he?
He must indeed, Agathon replied.

Then, said Socrates, he wants what he presently possesses to be kept for him in the future. That amounts to saying he desires something that does not exist for him now, something he does not yet have:
That is quite true, he said.

So he, like everyone who desires, desires what he does not already possess, what lies in the future rather than the present, what he neither has nor is, and what he lacks. Are these the kinds of things love and desire seek?
That is quite true, he said.
Now, said Socrates, let us go over the argument again. First, love is love of something, and of something the person lacks, is it not?
Yes, he answered.

Remember also what you said in your speech. If you have forgotten, I will remind you: you said love of the beautiful brought order to the gods’ kingdom, since there is no love of deformed things. Didn’t you say something like that?
Yes, Agathon replied.
Yes, my friend, and rightly so. If that is true, then Love loves beauty, not deformity, does he not?
He agreed.
And we have already agreed that Love is love of something a person lacks and does not possess?
That is true, he said.
Then Love lacks beauty and does not possess it?
Of course, he replied.
Would you call something beautiful if it lacks beauty and does not possess it?
Certainly I would not.
Would you still maintain, then, that love is beautiful?
Agathon replied: I am afraid I did not know what I was saying.
Your speech was very fine, Agathon, Socrates replied. But there is one more little question I would like to ask: is what is good not also beautiful?
Yes, it is.
Then, in lacking the beautiful, love also lacks the good?
I cannot disprove your argument, Socrates, said Agathon. Let us accept what you say as true.
Say instead, dear Agathon, that you cannot disprove the truth. Socrates himself is easy enough to refute.

Now I shall leave you and recount what I heard about love from Diotima of Mantineia (compare 1 Alcibiades), a woman wise in this subject and in many other fields. Long ago, when the Athenians sacrificed before the plague arrived, she delayed the disease for ten years. She taught me the art of love, and I shall repeat her words, beginning with Agathon’s admissions, which are almost, if not exactly, the same as those I made when that wise woman questioned me. This seems the easiest approach, and I shall play both parts myself as well as I can (compare Gorgias). As you suggested earlier, Agathon (supra), I must first explain Love’s being and nature, then his actions. I began by telling her, in almost the same words Agathon used to me, that Love was a powerful god and beautiful too. Just as I have shown Agathon, she showed me that my own account made Love neither beautiful nor good. 'What do you mean, Diotima?' I asked. 'Is love ugly and evil, then?' 'Hush,' she said. 'Must everything that is not beautiful be ugly?' 'Certainly,' I replied. 'And must whatever is not wise be ignorant? Don’t you see there is something between wisdom and ignorance?' 'What would that be?' I asked.

'Right opinion,' she answered. 'As you know, it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge—for how could knowledge lack reason? Yet it is not ignorance either, since ignorance cannot reach the truth. Clearly, then, it lies between ignorance and wisdom.' 'Quite true,' I said. 'So do not insist that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly, or whatever is not good must be evil. Nor should you conclude that because love is neither beautiful nor good, he is ugly and evil. He lies between the two.' 'Well,' I said, 'surely everyone agrees that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows, or everyone who does not know?' 'Everyone.' She smiled. 'How, Socrates, can people who say Love is not a god at all recognise him as a great god?' 'Who says that?' I asked. 'You and I are two who do,' she replied. 'How can that be?' 'It is easy to understand,' she answered. 'You yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful—of course you would. Would you dare say any god was not?' 'Certainly not,' I replied. 'And by happy, you mean those who possess good or beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'You admitted that Love desires good and beautiful things because he lacks them?' 'Yes, I did.' 'But how can someone with no share in what is good or beautiful be a god?' 'He cannot.' 'You see, then, that you too deny Love is divine.'

'What is Love, then?' I asked. 'Is he mortal?' 'No.' 'What, then?' 'As before, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but between the two.' 'What is he, Diotima?' 'A great spirit, a daimon. Like every spirit, he stands between the divine and the mortal.' 'What power does he have?' I asked. 'He interprets between gods and human beings,' she replied, 'carrying human prayers and sacrifices to the gods, and the gods’ commands and replies to human beings. He mediates across the gulf dividing them, binding everything together. Through him pass the arts of prophets and priests, their sacrifices, mysteries, and charms, and every prophecy and incantation. God does not mingle with humanity: all contact and conversation between God and human beings, asleep or awake, takes place through Love. Wisdom that understands this is spiritual; every other sort, such as skill in arts and crafts, is low and common. There are many different spirits, or intermediate powers, and Love is one of them.' 'Who were his father and mother?' I asked. 'It is a long story,' she said, 'but I will tell you. On Aphrodite’s birthday, the gods held a feast. Among the guests was Poros, or Plenty, son of Metis, or Discretion. When the feast ended, Penia, or Poverty, came begging at the doors, as happens on such occasions.

Plenty had drunk too much nectar—there was no wine then—and went into Zeus’ garden, where he fell into a deep sleep. Poverty, reflecting on her own desperate circumstances, plotted to have a child by him. She lay down beside him and conceived Love. He became Aphrodite’s follower and attendant partly because he naturally loves beauty and she is beautiful, and partly because he was born on her birthday. His fortunes reflect his parentage. First, he is always poor, and far from tender and beautiful as most people imagine. He is rough and dirty, barefoot and homeless, sleeping exposed on the bare ground under the open sky, in streets or at people’s doorways. Like his mother, he is always in need. Yet he partly resembles his father too: he is always scheming to capture the beautiful and good, bold, enterprising, strong, a formidable hunter, forever devising some intrigue, eager in the pursuit of wisdom, rich in resources, always a philosopher, a fearsome enchanter, sorcerer, and sophist. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal. At one moment, when he has plenty, he lives and flourishes; at another he dies, only to come alive again through his father’s nature.

Whatever flows in keeps flowing out, so he is never destitute and never wealthy. He also stands between ignorance and knowledge. Here is the truth: no god is a philosopher or seeker of wisdom, since a god is already wise; nor does any wise human being seek wisdom. But the ignorant do not seek wisdom either. That is the evil of ignorance: someone neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself and does not desire what he does not feel he lacks.' 'Who, then, Diotima, are the lovers of wisdom,' I asked, 'if they are neither wise nor foolish?' 'Even a child could answer that,' she said. 'Those between the two, and Love is one of them. Wisdom is supremely beautiful, and Love loves the beautiful. Love must therefore be a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and as such stand between the wise and the ignorant. His birth explains this too: his father is wealthy and wise, his mother poor and foolish. That, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistaken view was quite natural. From what you say, I imagine you confused love with the beloved, which made you think love was altogether beautiful. It is the beloved who is truly beautiful, delicate, perfect, and blessed. The principle of love has a different nature, the one I have described.'

I said, 'Lady from another land, you speak well. But if Love is as you describe him, what use is he to human beings?' 'That, Socrates,' she replied, 'is what I shall try to explain. I have already discussed his nature and birth, and you agree that love loves the beautiful. But someone might ask: in what sense the beautiful, Socrates and Diotima? Or, to put it more clearly, what does a man desire when he loves the beautiful?' I answered, 'To have the beautiful for himself.' 'Still,' she said, 'that answer raises another question: what does possessing beauty give him?' 'I have no answer ready for that,' I replied. 'Then let me replace the beautiful with the word "good" and ask again. If someone who loves loves the good, what does he love?' 'Possessing the good,' I said. 'And what does he gain by possessing it?' 'Happiness,' I replied. 'That question is easier to answer.' 'Yes,' she said. 'People become happy by acquiring good things. We need not go on to ask why someone wants happiness: the answer is already complete.' 'You are right,' I said.

'Does everyone share this wish and desire? Does everyone always want their own good, or only some people? What do you say?' 'Everyone,' I replied. 'The desire belongs to everyone.' 'Why, then, Socrates, do we say only some people love, rather than all of them, when you say they are all always loving the same things?' 'I wonder that myself,' I said. 'There is no mystery,' she answered. 'One part of love is singled out and given the name of the whole; the other parts receive different names.' 'Give me an example,' I said. She replied: 'Take poetry, which, as you know, has many forms and aspects. All creation, every passage from non-being into being, is poetry or making. The processes of every art are creative, and all masters of arts are poets or makers.' 'Quite true.' 'Yet you know they are not called poets,' she continued. 'They have other names. Only the part of this art separated from the rest and concerned with music and metre is called poetry, and those possessing poetry in that sense are called poets.' 'Quite true,' I said. 'Love works in the same way.

In general, you could say that every desire for goodness and happiness is the great, subtle power of love. But those who approach him by other routes—money-making, gymnastics, or philosophy—are not called lovers. The name of the whole is reserved for people whose affection takes just one particular form: only they are said to love, or to be lovers.' 'I think you are right,' I replied. 'Yes,' she went on, 'and you hear people say lovers search for their other half. But I say they seek neither half of themselves nor the whole, unless that half or whole is also good. People will even cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away if they are bad. They do not love something just because it is theirs—unless, perhaps, someone calls whatever is his own good and whatever belongs to someone else evil. People love nothing but the good. Do they?' 'I would certainly say they do not.' 'The simple truth, then,' she said, 'is that people love the good.' 'Yes,' I said. 'And must we add that they love to possess the good?' 'Yes, we must.' 'Not merely to possess it, but to possess it for ever?' 'We must add that too.' 'Then we may describe love generally as the love of possessing the good for ever?' 'That is entirely true.'

'If this is love’s nature,' she said, 'can you also explain how people pursue it? What are they doing when they show all this eagerness and passion we call love? What goal are they aiming at? Answer me.' 'Diotima,' I replied, 'if I knew, I would not have marvelled at your wisdom or come to learn this very thing from you.' 'Then I will teach you,' she said. 'Their aim is birth in beauty, whether in body or in soul.' 'I do not understand,' I said. 'That oracle needs interpreting.' 'I will make it clearer,' she replied. 'All human beings bring things to birth in their bodies and their souls. At a certain age, human nature desires procreation, which must take place in beauty, not deformity. This procreation is the union of man and woman, and it is divine: conception and generation are an immortal principle in a mortal creature, and they can never occur in what is out of harmony. Deformity is always out of harmony with the divine, whereas beauty is in harmony with it.

Beauty, then, is the destiny or goddess of childbirth who presides over birth. When the power of conception approaches beauty, it becomes favourable, expansive, and generous, begetting and bearing fruit. At the sight of ugliness, she frowns, contracts in pain, turns away, and shrivels, painfully holding back from conception. That is why, when the time for conception comes and the fertile nature is full, beauty causes such excitement and ecstasy: its approach relieves the pains of labour. For love, Socrates, is not simply love of the beautiful, as you suppose.' 'What is it, then?' 'Love of generation and birth in beauty.' 'Yes,' I said. 'Yes indeed,' she replied. 'But why generation?' 'Because for a mortal creature, generation is a kind of eternity and immortality,' she answered. 'If, as we have already agreed, love seeks to possess the good for ever, everyone must necessarily desire immortality together with goodness. Love therefore seeks immortality.'

She taught me all this at different times in our conversations about love. I remember her once asking, 'Socrates, what causes love and the desire accompanying it? Do you not see how all animals, birds and beasts alike, suffer when they catch the fever of love in their wish to reproduce? It begins with the desire to mate, followed by care for offspring. For their young, the weakest will fight the strongest to the very end, even die for them, torment themselves with hunger, or suffer anything to keep them alive. We might suppose human beings act this way from reason, but why do animals feel these passions? Can you tell me?' Again I said I did not know. She replied, 'And do you expect to master the art of love without knowing this?' 'Diotima, I have already told you that my ignorance is why I come to you. I know I need a teacher. Tell me the cause of this and of love’s other mysteries.' 'Do not be surprised,' she said, 'if you believe, as we have repeatedly agreed, that love seeks immortality. Here too, on the same principle, mortal nature tries to become everlasting and immortal as far as possible. It can achieve this only through generation, which always leaves a new existence behind in place of the old.

Even within one individual’s life there is succession, not absolute unity. We call a person the same person, yet in the brief interval between youth and old age—the period in which any animal is said to possess life and identity—he is continually losing and replacing things. Hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the entire body keep changing. This is true not just of the body but of the soul: habits, dispositions, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears never stay the same in any of us, but constantly come and go. Knowledge behaves in the same way. More surprising still to us mortals, not only do the sciences in general arise and decay, so that we never remain the same in relation to them, but each individual science changes in this way too. What does "recollection" imply except that knowledge departs? Knowledge is continually forgotten, then renewed and preserved through recollection, appearing the same although it is actually new. This follows the law of succession that preserves everything mortal through replacement rather than absolute sameness: old, worn-out mortality leaves behind another new existence like itself. The divine, by contrast, is always the same, never another. This, Socrates, is how a mortal body, or anything mortal, shares in immortality; what is immortal does so in a different way.
So do not be surprised by the love everyone feels for their offspring: that universal love and concern seek immortality.'

Astonished by her words, I asked, 'Wise Diotima, is this really true?' She answered with all the authority of an accomplished sophist: 'You may be sure of it, Socrates. Consider human ambition. People’s behaviour will seem senseless unless you see how the desire for immortal fame drives them. To leave an everlasting name, they will run risks far greater than they would for their children, spend their money, endure every kind of toil, and even die. Do you think Alcestis would have died to save Admetus, Achilles to avenge Patroclus, or your own Codrus to preserve the kingdom for his sons, had they not believed the memory of their virtues would be immortal—a memory still alive among us? No,' she said, 'I am convinced that everyone does everything in hope of the glorious fame of immortal virtue, and the better they are, the more they do. They desire what is immortal.

'Those pregnant only in body turn to women and father children. That is the form their love takes: they hope their offspring will preserve their memory and give them the future blessedness and immortality they desire. But pregnant souls—for some men certainly create more through their souls than through their bodies—conceive what it is proper for a soul to conceive and bear. What do they conceive? Wisdom and virtue in general. Poets and all artists worthy of being called inventors are such creators. By far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom, however, concerns the ordering of cities and households, and is called temperance and justice. Someone in whom these seeds are planted in youth, someone himself inspired, desires to beget and generate when he reaches maturity.

He roams in search of beauty in which to beget offspring, since he will beget nothing in deformity. Naturally, he embraces a beautiful body rather than a deformed one. Above all, when he finds a beautiful, noble, well-nurtured soul, he welcomes body and soul together in that one person. He has much to say to him about virtue and about a good man’s nature and pursuits, and tries to educate him. Through contact with the beautiful, which remains in his memory even when absent, he brings forth what he conceived long ago, and together they nurture what he produces. Their bond is much closer, their friendship more intimate, than that of people who produce mortal children, because the children they share are more beautiful and more immortal. Thinking of Homer, Hesiod, and other great poets, who would not prefer their children to ordinary human ones? Who would not want to create children like theirs, which preserved their memory and gave them everlasting glory? Or children like those Lycurgus left behind, saviours not merely of Lacedaemon but, one might say, of all Hellas?
