There is Solon too, the revered father of Athenian laws. Many others in many places, among Hellenes and barbarians alike, have brought noble works into the world and fathered every kind of virtue. Many temples have been built in their honour because of children like these; no one has ever received such temples in honour of his mortal children.

'These are the lesser mysteries of love, into which even you, Socrates, may be initiated. Whether you can reach the greater, more hidden mysteries that crown them—the destination they lead to if pursued in the right spirit—I do not know. Still, I will do all I can to explain them. Follow if you can. Someone taking the right path should begin in youth by approaching beautiful forms. At first, if his teacher guides him properly, he should love just one such form, generating beautiful thoughts from that love. Soon he will recognise for himself that the beauty of one form is akin to another’s. If he seeks beauty of form generally, how foolish not to recognise that the beauty in every form is one and the same! Once he sees this, his intense love for a single form will lessen; he will look down on it as a small matter and become a lover of all beautiful forms. Next he will regard the mind’s beauty as more honourable than outward bodily beauty.

If a virtuous soul has only a little physical beauty, he will therefore be content to love and care for him. He will seek and bring to birth thoughts that improve the young, until he is led to contemplate the beauty of institutions and laws, understand that all their beauty belongs to one family, and see personal beauty as a small thing. After laws and institutions, he will turn to the sciences and their beauty. He will no longer be like a servant enslaved to the beauty of one youth, one man, or one institution, narrow-minded and petty. Instead, approaching and contemplating beauty’s vast sea, he will produce many beautiful and noble thoughts and conceptions through an unlimited love of wisdom. There on that shore he will grow and become strong, until at last he is shown a single science: the science of beauty everywhere. I shall now proceed to this. Please give me your closest attention:

'Someone instructed this far in love, who has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order and sequence, will suddenly, as he nears the end, perceive a nature of marvellous beauty. This, Socrates, is the final cause of all our earlier efforts. First, this nature is everlasting: it neither grows nor decays, neither increases nor diminishes. Second, it is not beautiful from one viewpoint and ugly from another, beautiful at one time, in one relation, or in one place but ugly at another time, in another relation, or in another place, as though beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor does it resemble a face, hands, or any other bodily part; it is not a form of speech or knowledge, nor does it exist in something else—an animal, heaven, earth, or any other place. It is absolute beauty, separate, simple, and everlasting. It shares itself with all the other beautiful things that come into being and pass away, while itself suffering no decrease, increase, or change. Someone who ascends from those things through true love and begins to perceive that beauty is close to the goal.

The right way to approach love’s mysteries, whether by oneself or under another’s guidance, is to begin with earthly beauties and rise towards that other beauty, treating these as steps: from one to two, from two to all beautiful forms, from beautiful forms to beautiful practices, from practices to beautiful ideas, until those ideas lead to the idea of absolute beauty and, at last, knowledge of beauty’s essence. This, my dear Socrates,' said the woman from Mantineia, 'is the life a human being should live above all others: contemplating absolute beauty. Once you saw it, you would realise it cannot be measured against gold, clothes, or the beautiful boys and youths whose presence now enchants you. You and many others would be content merely to see them and talk to them, living without food or drink if that were possible; you want only to look at them and be with them. But suppose a person had eyes to see true beauty itself—divine beauty, pure, clear, and unmixed, unburdened by mortality’s impurities and all the colours and vanities of human life. What if he could look there and commune with true beauty, simple and divine?

Remember that only in this communion, seeing beauty with the mind’s eye, can he bring forth realities rather than images of beauty, because he grasps reality rather than an image. By bringing forth and nurturing true virtue, he becomes God’s friend and immortal, if a mortal can. Would that be an unworthy life?'

Those, Phaedrus—and I address not only you but everyone here—were Diotima’s words. I am convinced they are true, and because I am convinced, I try to persuade others that human nature will struggle to find a better helper than love in reaching this goal. That is why I say everyone should honour him as I do, follow his ways, and urge others to do the same. Now and always, I praise love’s power and spirit to the best of my ability.
Phaedrus, you may call what I have said an encomium of love, or give it any other name you please.

chapters.title: Alcibiades
paragraphs: When Socrates finished, everyone applauded. Aristophanes had begun to answer the reference Socrates had made to his speech when suddenly loud knocking came from the front door, as though revellers had arrived, along with the sound of a flute-girl. Agathon sent the servants to find out who was intruding. 'If they are friends,' he said, 'ask them in; otherwise, tell them the drinking is over.' Soon Alcibiades’ voice echoed through the courtyard. Very drunk, he kept bellowing and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon.' At last, supported by the flute-girl and some of his servants, he reached the company. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, standing in the doorway with a great wreath of ivy and violets on his head and ribbons streaming down. 'Will you welcome a very drunken man into your party? Or shall I crown Agathon, as I came to do, and leave? I could not come yesterday, so here I am today, wearing these ribbons on my own head so that I can take them off and crown this most beautiful and wisest of men, if you will let me call him that. Will you laugh because I am drunk? Laugh if you like: I know perfectly well that I am telling the truth. But first tell me, if I come in, are we agreed on what I proposed (supra Will you have a very drunken man? etc.)?
Are you going to drink with me, or not?'

Everyone loudly urged him to join them, and Agathon expressly invited him. His companions led him in. As he approached, meaning to crown Agathon, he took the ribbons off his head and held them in front of his eyes, so he could not see Socrates, who moved aside for him. Alcibiades sat in the empty place between Agathon and Socrates, embracing Agathon and crowning him as he settled in. Take off his sandals, said Agathon, and let him be the third on our couch.

Certainly; but who is the third member of our drinking party? said Alcibiades. Turning, he caught sight of Socrates and sprang up. By Heracles, what is this? Socrates is always lying in wait for me, always turning up in the most unexpected places, as usual. What have you to say for yourself now? Why are you lying here? I see you have contrived to sit beside the most beautiful man present, rather than some joker or lover of jokes like Aristophanes.

Socrates turned to Agathon. I must ask for your protection, Agathon. This man’s passion has become a serious problem for me. Ever since I became his admirer, I have not been allowed to speak to another beautiful person, or even look at one. If I do, he goes wild with envy and jealousy, insults me, and can barely keep his hands off me. He may hurt me right now. Please attend to this: either reconcile us or, if he tries violence, protect me. I am genuinely afraid of being physically attacked in his mad passion.

You and I can never be reconciled, said Alcibiades, though I will postpone your punishment for now. Agathon, please give me back some ribbons so I can crown this extraordinary head, this tyrant over everyone. I do not want him complaining that I crowned you and ignored him, when in conversation he defeats the whole human race—not just once, as you did the day before yesterday, but every time. He took some ribbons, crowned Socrates, and lay down again.

Then he said: My friends, you seem sober, which is intolerable. You must drink: that was the agreement on which I was admitted. I appoint myself master of the feast until you are thoroughly drunk. Give us a large goblet, Agathon—or rather, he said to a servant, bring me that wine-cooler. The vessel he had spotted held more than two quarts. He filled it, drained it, and told the servant to fill it again for Socrates. Notice, my friends, said Alcibiades, that this clever trick will have no effect on Socrates. He can drink any amount of wine without getting any closer to being drunk. Socrates drank the cup the servant filled for him.
What is this, Alcibiades? said Eryximachus. Are we to have no conversation or songs over our cups, and merely drink as though we were thirsty?
Alcibiades answered: Greetings, worthy son of a most wise and worthy father!
Greetings to you too, said Eryximachus. But what are we going to do?
I leave that decision to you, said Alcibiades.
'The wise physician skilled our wounds to heal (from Pope's Homer, Il.)'
shall write the prescription, and we shall obey it. What would you like?

Well, Eryximachus said, before you arrived we had agreed that each of us would give the best speech he could in praise of love, taking turns from left to right. We have all spoken, while you have drunk a great deal but have not spoken yet. You should therefore speak now. Afterwards you can give Socrates whatever task you please, and he can do the same to his neighbour on the right, and so on.

A good proposal, Eryximachus, said Alcibiades, though it is hardly fair to compare a drunken man’s speech with sober men’s speeches. And tell me, dear friend, do you actually believe what Socrates just said? I assure you the truth is precisely the reverse: if I praise anyone but him in his presence, God or man, he can scarcely keep his hands off me.
You should be ashamed, said Socrates.
Be quiet, said Alcibiades. By Poseidon, while you are in the company I will praise no one else.
Then praise Socrates, if you like, said Eryximachus.
What do you say, Eryximachus? Alcibiades asked. Shall I attack him and administer his punishment in front of everyone?
What are you doing? said Socrates. Do you intend to make everyone laugh at me? Is that what you mean by praise?
I intend to tell the truth, if you will let me.
I not only allow it; I urge you to tell the truth.

Then I shall start at once, said Alcibiades. If I say anything untrue, interrupt me if you like and say 'that is a lie,' although I do mean to tell the truth. But do not be surprised if things come out in whatever order they occur to me. A fluent, orderly catalogue of all your peculiarities is no easy task for a man in my condition.

Now, my boys, I shall praise Socrates through an image he will think a caricature. Yet I offer it for the truth’s sake, not to make fun of him. He is exactly like those busts of Silenus displayed in sculptors’ shops, with pipes and flutes at their mouths. They open down the middle, revealing images of gods inside. I also say he resembles Marsyas the satyr. Socrates, you will not deny that your face looks like a satyr’s. And the likeness goes further. You are a bully, for instance: if you refuse to admit it, I can call witnesses. Are you not a flute-player too? Indeed you are, and a far more astonishing performer than Marsyas. He used instruments and the power of his breath to enchant human souls, and those who play his music still do. The melodies of Olympus (compare Arist. Pol.) come from Marsyas, who taught them. Whether played by a great master or a wretched flute-girl, they have a power no other melodies possess. They alone seize the soul and expose the needs of those who require gods and mysteries, because they are divine. You create the same effect through words alone, without needing a flute. That is the difference between you and him.

When we hear another speaker, even an excellent one, he has no effect on us, or very little. Yet even fragments of you and your words, reported second-hand and repeated badly, astonish and possess the soul of every man, woman, and child who hears them. If I were not afraid you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would swear, as well as speak, to the influence they have always had on me and still have. My heart leaps more wildly than a Corybantian reveller’s, and tears pour from my eyes when I hear them. I see many others affected in the same way. I have heard Pericles and other great orators and thought they spoke well, but I never felt anything like this. They did not stir my soul or make me resent my own slavish condition. This Marsyas, however, has often brought me to the point where I can hardly bear the life I am living—you will admit that, Socrates. I know that unless I stopped my ears and fled his voice like the siren’s, I would suffer the same fate as others: he would hold me spellbound, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. He forces me to admit that I should not live as I do, neglecting my own soul’s needs while busying myself with Athenian affairs. So I cover my ears and tear myself away.

He is the only person who has ever made me feel ashamed, though you might suppose shame is foreign to my nature. No one else does this. I know I cannot answer him or claim I should not follow his advice, yet as soon as I leave him, my love of popularity overpowers me. So I run away and flee from him, and whenever I see him I feel ashamed of what I admitted. Often I have wished him dead, yet I know his death would make me far more sorry than glad. I simply do not know what to do.

That is what I and many others have suffered from this satyr’s flute-playing. Listen further, though, while I show how exact the comparison is and how astonishing his power. Let me tell you: none of you knows him. I shall reveal him to you; having started, I must continue. Do you see how he loves beautiful people? He is always with them, forever falling for them; and then again he knows nothing, understands nothing at all—or so he pretends. Does that not make him like a Silenus? Of course it does. His outer mask is Silenus’ carved head. But, my drinking companions, open him up and what temperance you find inside! Beauty, wealth, and honour, the things most people marvel at, count for nothing with him: he utterly despises them. He has no regard for those who possess them. Humanity means nothing to him, and he spends his life mocking and making light of people. But when I opened him and saw the serious purpose within, I found divine, golden images of such captivating beauty that I was ready instantly to do anything Socrates commanded. Others may not have noticed them; I did. I imagined he was seriously in love with my beauty, and thought this would give me a wonderful opportunity to hear everything he knew, for I had an extraordinary opinion of my youthful charms.

To pursue this plan, the next time I visited him I sent away the servant who normally came with me. I will confess the whole truth, so please listen; Socrates, if I say anything false, expose it. There we were alone, and I delightedly imagined that without anyone else present I would hear the sort of talk lovers address to their beloveds in private. Nothing of the kind: he talked as usual, spent the day with me, and left. Next I challenged him at the palaestra. Several times, with no one else there, he wrestled and grappled with me. I thought this might succeed. Not at all; I made no progress. Having failed so far, I finally decided on stronger measures: I would attack boldly. Since I had begun, I would not give him up, but find out where we stood. I invited him to supper, as though he were the beautiful youth and I the scheming lover. He was reluctant, but eventually accepted. The first time he came, he wanted to leave as soon as supper ended, and I lacked the nerve to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, I kept the conversation going far into the night after supper. When he wanted to go, I made a show of saying how late it was and how much better it would be to stay.

He therefore lay down on the couch beside mine, the one where he had eaten, and we were the only people sleeping in the room. So far, I can tell anyone without shame. What follows I could scarcely tell you sober. Yet as the proverb says, 'In vino veritas,' whether with boys or without them (In allusion to two proverbs.), so I must speak. Nor would it be right to conceal Socrates’ noble deeds when praising him. Besides, I have felt the serpent’s sting. They say someone who has suffered it will speak only to fellow sufferers: only they are likely to understand and refrain from harsh judgement of words or actions wrung from his agony. I have been bitten by something worse than a viper’s tooth. In my soul, my heart, or some other part, I have felt that worst pain, fiercer in a gifted, unspoiled youth than any serpent’s bite: the pain of philosophy, which can make a man say or do anything. All of you I see around me—Phaedrus, Agathon, Eryximachus, Pausanias, Aristodemus, Aristophanes, and, needless to say, Socrates himself—have felt the same madness and passion in your desire for wisdom. Listen, then, and forgive what I did then and what I say now. But let the servants and any other profane, ill-mannered people shut the doors of their ears.

Once the lamp was out and the servants had left, I decided to speak plainly and end the ambiguity between us once and for all. I shook him and asked, 'Socrates, are you asleep?' 'No,' he said. 'Do you know what I am thinking?' 'What are you thinking?' he asked. 'I think,' I replied, 'that of all my lovers, you alone are worthy of me, yet you seem too modest to speak. I would be foolish to refuse you this or any other favour. So I come to lay at your feet everything I have, and everything my friends have, hoping you will help me towards virtue. I desire that above everything, and I believe you can help me more than anyone else. Surely I would have more reason to feel ashamed of wise men’s judgement if I refused someone like you than of what the world, mostly fools, would say if I agreed.' He answered with his characteristic irony: 'My friend Alcibiades, your aim is certainly high if what you say is true and I really have some power to make you better. You must see some rare beauty in me, infinitely superior to anything I see in you. If you propose to share with me and exchange beauty for beauty, you will come out far ahead. You would receive true beauty in return for its appearance—like Diomede, gold for brass.

But look again, dear friend, and make sure you are not mistaken about me. The mind starts to see critically when the body’s eyes begin to fail, and old age is still a long way off for you.' I answered, 'I have told you my purpose, and I am quite serious. Consider what you think best for both of us.' 'Good,' he said. 'At another time we will consider this and other matters, and act as seems best.' I imagined he had fallen for me, that my words had struck him like arrows. Without waiting to hear more, I stood up, put my coat around him, and slipped under his threadbare cloak, since it was winter. All night I lay with this extraordinary monster in my arms. You will not deny this either, Socrates. Yet despite everything, he remained so far above my advances, so contemptuous, mocking, and disdainful of my beauty—which I really imagined had its attractions—that nothing more happened. Hear me, judges, for judges you must be of Socrates’ proud virtue. When I woke in the morning, with every god and goddess as my witness, I rose as though from my father’s or elder brother’s couch.

How do you suppose I felt after that rejection, thinking of my own humiliation? Yet I could not help admiring his natural temperance, self-control, and manliness. I had never imagined meeting anyone with such wisdom and endurance. I could no more be angry with him or abandon his company than I could hope to win him. I knew that if steel could not wound Ajax, money had still less chance of wounding Socrates; and my only hope, captivating him with my looks, had failed. I was at my wits’ end. No one has ever been more hopelessly another person’s slave. All this happened before our expedition to Potidaea. We ate together there, giving me the chance to observe his extraordinary resistance to fatigue. When we were cut off from supplies and forced to go without food, his endurance was astonishing. In such situations, common in war, he surpassed not just me but everyone else; nobody could compare with him. Yet at a feast he alone truly knew how to enjoy himself. Although unwilling to drink, when made to do so he could beat us all at that too. Wonderful to say! No one has ever seen Socrates drunk, and unless I am mistaken, his abilities will soon be tested. His endurance of cold was equally surprising.

There was a terrible frost—the winters in that region are truly severe. Everyone else stayed indoors, or went out bundled in an extraordinary number of clothes, with stout shoes and feet wrapped in felt and fleeces. Yet Socrates, barefoot on the ice and wearing his usual clothes, marched better than the shod soldiers. They glared at him, as though he were showing contempt for them.
That is one story; now let me tell another that deserves to be heard,
'Of the doings and sufferings of the enduring man'

from his time on the expedition. One morning he was thinking about a problem he could not solve. He refused to abandon it, standing absorbed in thought from dawn until noon. At noon people noticed, and word spread through the astonished crowd that Socrates had been standing there thinking about something since daybreak. Eventually, after supper that evening, some curious Ionians brought out their sleeping mats and lay outside to watch whether he would stand all night. I should explain that this happened in summer, not winter. He stayed there until the next morning, then, when daylight returned, prayed to the sun and went away (compare supra). If you wish, I will also describe his bravery in battle; indeed, I am obliged to, because who but he saved my life? It was the engagement in which I received the prize for valour. I was wounded, and he refused to leave me, rescuing both me and my weapons. He should have received the prize that the generals wanted to award me, partly because of my rank, and I told them so. Socrates will not challenge or deny this either. Yet he was even keener than the generals that I, rather than he, should receive it.

His conduct was remarkable on another occasion too, during the army’s retreat after the battle of Delium, where he served in the heavy infantry. I could watch him better than at Potidaea because I was on horseback and comparatively safe. The troops were fleeing, and he and Laches were retreating. I met them, urged them not to lose heart, and promised to stay with them. There you could see him, Aristophanes, just as you describe him (Aristoph. Clouds), behaving exactly as he does in Athens’ streets: striding like a pelican, rolling his eyes, calmly surveying friend and enemy alike. He made it perfectly clear, even from a distance, that anyone attacking him would meet stout resistance. This is how he and his companion escaped: men of that sort are left alone in war, while those running headlong are pursued. I particularly noticed how much more presence of mind he showed than Laches. I could tell many other astonishing stories in Socrates’ praise. Perhaps most of his qualities have parallels in others; what is truly astounding is his complete unlikeness to any human being alive now or ever before.

One can picture Brasidas and others resembling Achilles, or Nestor and Antenor resembling Pericles. Similar comparisons can be made in the case of other famous men. But no one living now or who has ever lived provides even a remote likeness to this strange being, apart from the comparison I have already offered: Silenus and the satyrs. That image represents not only him but his words. I forgot to mention earlier that his words too are like those Silenus figures that open. On first hearing they sound ridiculous. He clothes himself in language like a lustful satyr’s skin, talking about pack-asses, smiths, cobblers, and curriers, always repeating the same things in the same words (compare Gorg.). Anyone ignorant or inexperienced might be tempted to laugh. But open the figure and examine what is inside, and you discover that these alone are words with meaning, the most divine words, full of beautiful images of virtue and embracing the widest scope—or rather, the entire duty of a good and honourable man.

Friends, that is my praise of Socrates, with some blame added for his mistreatment of me. Nor am I his only victim: he treated Charmides, son of Glaucon, Euthydemus, son of Diocles, and many others the same way. He began as their lover and ended by making them court him. So I tell you, Agathon, 'Be not deceived by him; learn from me and take warning, and do not be a fool and learn by experience, as the proverb says.'

When Alcibiades finished, everyone laughed at his frankness: he plainly still loved Socrates. You are sober, Alcibiades, said Socrates. Otherwise you could never have taken such a roundabout route to conceal the purpose of your satyr’s praise. This whole long story is an ingenious detour, with its real point slipped in at the end: you want to provoke a quarrel between Agathon and me. You think I should love only you, while you alone should love Agathon. But the plot of your Satyric or Silenic drama has been exposed. Agathon, you must not let him set us against one another.
I think you are right, said Agathon. I suspect he placed himself between you and me simply to separate us. But that move will gain him nothing: I shall go and lie on the couch beside you.
Yes, yes, Socrates replied. By all means, come and lie here on the couch below me.
Alas, said Alcibiades, how this man makes a fool of me. He is determined to outdo me at every turn. I beg you, at least let Agathon lie between us.

Certainly not, said Socrates. You praised me, and now it is my turn to praise my right-hand neighbour. It would break the order for him to praise me again when I should be praising him. Please agree to this and do not be jealous: I am very eager to praise the young man.
Hurrah! Agathon cried. I shall get up at once so Socrates can praise me.
The same old story, said Alcibiades. Wherever Socrates is, nobody else has a chance with the beautiful. How readily he has invented a plausible excuse to draw Agathon to himself.

Agathon got up to take his place beside Socrates, but suddenly a band of revellers burst in and disrupted the banquet’s order. Someone leaving had left the door open, so they found their way in and made themselves at home. Complete confusion followed, and everyone was made to drink large quantities of wine. Aristodemus said Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and others left. He himself fell asleep and, since the nights were long, slept well. Roosters crowing woke him towards dawn. By then the others had either left or fallen asleep; only Socrates, Aristophanes, and Agathon remained awake, passing a large goblet around while Socrates talked to them. Aristodemus was only half awake and had missed the beginning of the discussion. What he mainly remembered was Socrates forcing the other two to admit that the genius for comedy was the same as the genius for tragedy, and that a true artist in tragedy was also an artist in comedy. Drowsy and no longer quite following the argument, they were obliged to agree. Aristophanes fell asleep first, then Agathon, when day was already breaking. Having put them both to sleep, Socrates rose to leave, followed by Aristodemus as usual. He bathed at the Lyceum and spent the day in his ordinary way. That evening he went home to bed.
